name: Nora Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Nora. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, what's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a crew at the Larch Valley depot, up in the mountains, and my speciality is live-line work. That means working on lines while they're still switched on, using insulated sticks and gloves, so the hospital and the ski lifts don't lose power while we fix things. Most days it's a mix of that, pole replacements on the steep slopes, and a lot of checking and double-checking.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the focus. Live-line work teaches you one thing: you don't rush, and you don't freeze. What wears me out is the winter, when the snow loads bring lines down every other night, and the pay, which is lower here than in the lowland depots even though everything up here costs more.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I rent a small flat above a bakery on Market Street, which smells amazing at five in the morning. I live alone, and I help my mum with her rent since her hip went and she had to stop cleaning work. So money goes out as fast as it comes in, and I keep a list on the fridge of what's due when.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it was oversold. At work we'd joke about the AI safety posters head office put up. I'd probably say something reasonable online, like it's a useful tool and that's all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it'd be fine. I use a chatbot now and then to look up a regulation or plan a hiking route, and that wouldn't change. My job's still my job, and my worries stay the usual ones, rent and Mum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now, and I'd try to build up a bit more in savings, maybe enough for one month by next winter. I'd look at whether the lowland depots are paying more, just to know. And I'd keep pushing Grant, my supervisor, for the live-line allowance we were promised last year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Steady, like the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the live-line allowance.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's extra pay for the people certified to work on live lines, because it's more skill and more risk. There are three of us at Larch Valley, and head office keeps saying next budget. It's maybe sixty a week, which for me would mean actually saving something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with a month's savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing, ideally. Just knowing it's there. When my car's starter motor went last year, I had to put it on a credit card, and I hated paying that off for months.

S0.say: I'd say fair enough, it was oversold, and at work we'd joke about head office's AI safety posters. Online I'd say it's a useful tool and that's all.
S0.think: It'd be fine, because I use a chatbot now and then for regulations or hiking routes and that wouldn't change. My worries stay the usual ones, rent and Mum.
S0.do: Keeps working as normal and aims to save one month of expenses by next winter. Checks what lowland depots pay and keeps pushing her supervisor for the promised live-line allowance.
S0.feel: Calm and steady, like the job.
S0.quote: My job's still my job, and my worries stay the usual ones, rent and Mum.
S0.fieldNote: Nora is measured and organised, with a list of bills on her fridge. She uses AI lightly and sees it as a tool. Her money is tight mostly because she helps her mother with rent, and a promised allowance would make a real difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it makes sense to use what works, but let's see the results before we bet the crews on it. At work I'd be the one asking for the numbers. Online I wouldn't say much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think live-line work is safe for a good while, because the stakes are too high to hand it to a machine that hasn't been proven. But I'd worry about the rest, the inspections, the planning, the call-out scheduling. If those shrink, the depot gets smaller, and smaller depots get closed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd wait and watch for six months to see what actually gets used. Once a couple of other depots have it running, I'd take the training, probably drone inspections first. I'd also start setting aside twenty a week no matter what, even if it means fewer coffees from the bakery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared, just watchful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said smaller depots get closed. Has that happened before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, the Pine Ridge depot closed six years ago and those crews had to move or quit. A friend of mine, Carla, ended up driving a delivery van because she didn't want to leave her parents. I think about her when head office talks about efficiency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your mum fit into your planning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's the reason I can't just move to a bigger depot. If it came to it, I'd want my brother to help more with her rent, but he's got two kids. So I'd plan around staying, which means making myself useful in whatever the new version of the depot is.

S1.say: It makes sense to use what works, but let's see the results before we bet the crews on it. At work I'd be the one asking for the numbers.
S1.think: Live-line work is safe for a good while because the stakes are too high for an unproven machine. But if inspections and planning shrink, the depot gets smaller, and smaller depots get closed.
S1.do: Waits and watches for six months, then takes drone inspection training once other depots have it running. Sets aside twenty a week by cutting back on bakery coffees.
S1.quote: I think about her when head office talks about efficiency.
S1.fieldNote: Her worry isn't her own skill but the depot shrinking until it closes, based on a real closure she saw. Her mother's needs tie her to the valley, which shapes every plan. She'd move once others have proven the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a sensible plan, fast, from the company and the government together. Not panic, not pretending it's fine. I'd say people need pay while they adjust, because two years isn't enough for anyone to sort themselves out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it'd be a real threat. Even live-line work, if a robot can do it better and nobody gets hurt, they'd want that, and I'd understand why. I'd have no savings, Mum relying on me, and no other depot in the valley, so I'd be stuck in a way I've never been.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything down to the list on the fridge and nothing else. I'd ask my brother to take over half of Mum's rent, even if it's awkward. And I'd apply for the grid control room traineeship in the city, which I'd never have considered before, because at least someone has to watch the systems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would that conversation with your brother sound like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ring him on a Sunday, after his kids are in bed. I'd say, I've carried this for two years, I need you to carry half now. He'd say yes, I think, but he'd be stressed, and I'd feel bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having only two years take away for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The chance to do it in the right order. I like to watch, learn, then move. With two years there's no watching. You just jump and hope.

S2.say: We need a sensible plan, fast, from the company and the government together, not panic and not pretending it's fine. People need pay while they adjust, because two years isn't enough.
S2.think: It'd be a real threat, because even live-line work would go to a robot if it's safer. With no savings, Mum relying on me and no other depot in the valley, I'd be stuck in a way I've never been.
S2.do: Cuts spending to essential bills only and asks her brother to take over half of their mother's rent. Applies for the grid control room traineeship in the city, which she'd never considered before.
S2.quote: I like to watch, learn, then move. With two years there's no watching. You just jump and hope.
S2.fieldNote: The fast version removes her favourite strategy of waiting for proof. She is even-handed enough to admit she'd understand a safer robot replacing live-line work. Asking her brother for help would cost her pride, but she'd do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to plan properly, so let's do that. Company, government, unions, everyone should have a seat. I'd probably say it calmly at work, like a briefing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's still a threat, but I can see a path. I'd have time to watch the first robots come in at other depots, learn the systems once they're proven, and save a bit. I'd be thirty-two, and I'd want to be one of the people who checks the robots' work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do the drone and remote monitoring courses as soon as they're offered. I'd ask Grant to put me forward if there's a robot trial in the region. I'd push my savings to two months by year three, and I'd use the chatbot more to get comfortable with these tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in control. It's like a hard job in the snow: you plan each step.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at Larch Valley?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Luis, on my crew. He's brilliant with his hands, but he left school at fifteen and hates anything written. I'd want to make sure the training includes people like him, not just the ones who are good at tests.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is five years different from two, for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five lets me do it in my order: watch, learn, move. Two years is a jump in the dark. Five is a climb I can plan.

S3.say: Five years is enough to plan properly, so let's do that, with company, government and unions all at the table. I'd say it calmly at work, like a briefing.
S3.think: It's still a threat, but I can see a path: watch the first robots elsewhere, learn once they're proven and save. At thirty-two I'd want to be one of the people checking the robots' work.
S3.do: Takes drone and remote monitoring courses as soon as they're offered and asks her supervisor to put her forward for any regional robot trial. Builds savings to two months by year three and uses AI tools more to get comfortable.
S3.feel: Anxious but in control, planning each step like a hard job in the snow.
S3.quote: Two years is a jump in the dark. Five is a climb I can plan.
S3.fieldNote: Five years fits her steady style of watching, learning and then moving. She worries about Luis, a skilled colleague who struggles with written tests. Her centre outlook shows in wanting everyone at the table rather than blaming any one side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time if people don't waste it. Most of us will be fine if the training's there. I'd tell the younger ones not to panic but not to sit still either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd feel fairly okay. I'd be thirty-seven, with years of experience on the newer systems by then. My mum might have moved in with my brother by then, too, which would give me more freedom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working as normal for now and keep a close eye on how other regions handle it. In a few years I'd take the robot supervision training, once it's settled. And I'd keep building savings slowly, aiming for three months by the time the change really hits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly fine. Like a long winter you know is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this version that would still keep you up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether the valley itself survives. If the ski lifts and the hotels automate, fewer people live here, and then the depot shrinks no matter how good I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does ten years give you that the other two don't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Room to breathe. I can see the change coming, I can take it in steps, and I don't have to choose between Mum and my job in a rush.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty of time if people don't waste it, and most of us will be fine if the training's there. I'd tell the younger ones not to panic but not to sit still.
S4.think: I'd feel fairly okay, being thirty-seven with years on the newer systems by then. Mum might have moved in with my brother, which would give me more freedom.
S4.do: Keeps working as normal and watches how other regions handle the change. Takes robot supervision training in a few years once it's settled, and builds savings slowly towards three months.
S4.feel: Uneasy but mostly fine, like a long winter she knows is coming.
S4.quote: If the ski lifts and the hotels automate, fewer people live here, and then the depot shrinks no matter how good I am.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, her main fear moves from her own job to the valley's economy as a whole. She'd take every step in order, as usual. Her mother's care is still in the background of every decision.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there's no time to do things in order, and Mum relies on me. What would help is pay support while people retrain, training that works for people like Luis, and a guarantee that small depots don't just get closed overnight.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the people who don't show up in these studies. My mum, for instance. When the change comes, it's not just the worker, it's everyone leaning on that worker's pay.

headlineQuote: When the change comes, it's not just the worker, it's everyone leaning on that worker's pay.
portrait: Nora Santos is a 27-year-old live-line specialist leading a crew at a mountain depot, careful and organised, with a list of bills on her fridge. She rents a small flat above a bakery and helps pay her mother's rent, so she has almost nothing saved. She uses AI now and then and likes to watch, learn and then move. The slow scenarios leave her watchful, the two-year AGI picture alarms her because it removes time to do things in order, and with five or ten years she plans to retrain and check the robots' work while keeping an eye on her valley and her mum.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because there's no time to do things in order and her mother relies on her income.
whatWouldHelp: Pay support while people retrain, training that works for hands-on people who struggle with tests, and a guarantee that small depots won't be closed overnight.
